newsitem.title: USA: Vote on Edison nuclear mitigation seen Tues.
newsitem.headline: Vote on Edison nuclear mitigation seen Tues.

text.p: California's Coastal Commission is expected to decide Tuesday on a bid by Edison International's Southern California Edison Co to reduce environmental mitigation requirements associated with the San Onofre nuclear power plant.

In response to environmental concerns, Edison agreed in 1991 to construct a 300-acre artificial kelp reef off the coast of southern California in order to mitigate damage from the plant's water intake and discharge systems.
But the company now says scientific tests indicate damage to the kelp beds is much less than expected.
Instead of the larger reef project, Edison is seeking clearance to build a much smaller 17-acre experimental kelp reef offshore San Clemente, Calif.

But the staff of the Coastal Commission proposed a compromise plan for a 122-acre reef, which would include the 17-acre experimental reef, to be funded by proceeds from a $19.27 million trust fund paid for by Edison, said commission spokeswoman Susan Hansch.

But Edison spokesman Clarence Brown said the company disagrees with the staff assessment of damage. "The kelp bed is intact and in healthy condition. We are committed to mitigating damage, but disagree over the amount."
Edison stresses that it has already spent millions of dollars on environmental mitigation efforts, such as fish hatcheries, associated with the nuclear plant.

But environmental groups maintain Edison's latest proposal has more to do with cost-consciousness amid deregulation of the electricity industry than it has to do with a change in scientific realities.

Edison owns 75 percent of the San Onofre project, which consists of one 1,070 unit and on 1,080 unit. Enova Corp's San Diego Gas and Electric Co holds a 20 percent stake in the plant and several municipal utilities share the remaining five percent.
